e.etymology: An elaboration of Sara or Sarah, Hebrew for princess, close to Sariah, a name from the Book of Mormon. Arabic has a similar name, Sariya, and Saria is also a character in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

assoc.t: Saria, Link's friend in Zelda: Ocarina of Time

e.etymology: A respelling of Trace, an English word name that began as a short form of Tracy, a surname from a place in Normandy.
From Kodiak Island in Alaska, home of the Kodiak brown bear. The island's name comes through Russian from the Alutiiq word qikertaq, island.

assoc.t: Kodiak bear, the giant Alaskan brown bear
Kodiak Cakes pancake and waffle mixes

e.etymology: An English surname, in most cases from a place name, used as a first name in the US by the early 1900s. Today it also recalls basketball star James Harden.

assoc.t: James Harden, bearded NBA star and former MVP

e.note: Also an ordinary English verb, and close in sound to a crude slang term, so some teasing is likely.

e.etymology: A modern name used in Hispanic families, a variation on Dayana, the Spanish phonetic spelling of Diana, alongside Dayanara and Dayami.
A modern American coinage, often written D'Mari, that sets the D- or De- prefix before Mari, in the family of Amari, Jamari and Damari.
A Latin American form in the family of Noelia and Noelle, feminine forms of French Noel, Christmas, from Latin natalis, of birth.
From Arabic dunya, the world, meaning this earthly life; a girls' name in Arabic, Turkish and Persian. In Russian, Dunya is a separate pet form of Avdotya, a form of Eudokia.

From Hindi and Urdu naksh, features or design, a word that came through Persian from Arabic naqsh, an engraving or imprint. It spread in the 2010s after a child character in the Hindi serial Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai.
A recent spelling used mainly in Hispanic families, close to Aliza, Eliza and Aleyda. Its source is not settled.
A recent American coinage that adds A- to Mylah, in the manner of Amyra and Amiyah.
A recent name from Spanish-speaking families, an elaboration of Lia or Liana with the -ny ending also seen in Arianny and Eliany.
An Indian spelling of Kiaan or Kian. The Persian name Kian means kings, from kay, the royal title of the legendary Kayanian dynasty. Kian is also a separate Irish name, a form of Cian.
In the US mostly an elaboration of Luna, Latin and Spanish for moon. Aluna is also a rare Welsh name, the feminine of Alun.
A recent Indian coinage that joins Kiyan to the ending -ansh, from Sanskrit amsha, a part or portion, as in Reyansh and Shivansh.
A recent name used mainly in Hispanic families, one of several spellings alongside Ailany and Aylani. Its sound follows Leilani and Kailani, Hawaiian names built on lani, sky or heaven.
The name of Swedish R&B singer Snoh Aalegra, born in Sweden to Persian parents. American use of the name dates from her rise around 2019.

e.meaning: ruler's counsel (Ronald); in Hebrew, song of joy
e.etymology: A short form of Ronald, the Scottish form of Old Norse Rognvaldr, from words for counsel and ruler. Ron is also an independent Hebrew name meaning joy or song.
namesakes: Ron Howard (director and former child actor)
e.note: Ron is the Spanish word for rum.

assoc.t: Ron Weasley, Harry Potter's best friend

e.etymology: The French spelling of Lucille, from Latin Lucilla, a pet form of Lucia, built on lux, light. It was fashionable in the US around 1900, helped by Owen Meredith's popular 1860 verse novel Lucile.
A spelling of Chelsea, the London district whose Old English name means chalk landing place, a wharf on the Thames. Chelsea became a girls' name in the 1970s and peaked in the early 1990s.
A spelling of Carrie, the pet form of Caroline, a feminine of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man. Cari is also a Welsh name from caru, to love.
A spelling of Darcy, a Norman surname, d'Arcy, for someone from Arcy in northern France. Jane Austen's Mr. Darcy made the surname famous; its use for girls is a 20th-century development.
namesakes: Darci Lynne (ventriloquist who won America's Got Talent)

e.etymology: A respelling of Derek, the English form of Low German and Dutch Diederik, from Theodoric, an old Germanic name meaning ruler of the people.
The Italian and Spanish form of Latin Faustus, a Roman family name from faustus, fortunate or auspicious, later borne by early Christian saints.

The Scottish spelling of Graham, a surname brought north from Grantham in Lincolnshire, whose Old English name means gravelly homestead. This spelling is common in Scotland, Australia and New Zealand.
The modern Greek form of Demetrios, belonging to Demeter, the goddess of grain and harvest. Saint Demetrius of Thessaloniki made it one of the most common Greek names.
From Arabic rashid, rightly guided or mature, from a verb meaning to follow the right path. Al-Rashid is one of the names of God in Islam, and Harun al-Rashid is the caliph of the Arabian Nights.

The German form of Theodoric, from Germanic words for people and ruler; Derek and Dirk are relatives. Dietrich von Bern, hero of medieval German legend, is based on the Gothic king Theodoric the Great.
namesakes: Dietrich Bonhoeffer (German pastor executed for resisting the Nazis)

assoc.t: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, pastor executed by the Nazis

e.etymology: A spelling of Dimitri, the Russian and French form of Greek Demetrios, belonging to Demeter, the goddess of grain and harvest.
A surname used as a first name, in most cases a spelling of Harlan, an English place name usually read as hare land. It was in use in the US by the 1880s.
The name of Saint Verena of Zurzach, a saint of the 3rd or 4th century venerated in Switzerland; its origin and meaning are obscure. It is common in Switzerland, Germany and Austria.
From Irish Tiarnan, a diminutive of tiarna, lord. It was borne by medieval Irish kings and saints and gave the surname Tiernan.
